pricing_unit.summary: The buyer commits to a multi-year spend floor, then burns it down on GPU hours and managed inference.

cluster_objections: If we commit to a three-year spend floor and our GPU utilization drops below plan, what happens to that commitment?
Your price per token looks fine, but how do we compare it with the committed-use discount we already have elsewhere?

marquee_lineage.label: AWS Cloud Economics and Marketplace Co-Sell

market_map.competition: Hyperscalers bundle model access into existing cloud commits, while GPU clouds like CoreWeave win on raw capacity and price per hour.

cards.title: Where it sits
cards.body: Compute is the bottom of the AI stack: the GPUs and cloud capacity every model and agent runs on.

cards.title: What the customer pays for
cards.body: Multi-year capacity commitments. The buyer reserves capacity before they use it.

cards.title: How the money works
cards.body: Capacity sold ahead of use. If the customer under-uses a commit, renewal becomes a churn risk.

cards.title: What threatens the deal
cards.body: Hyperscaler lock-in, raw price-per-FLOP comparisons, and competitors hoarding reserved capacity.

quiz.prompt: What does a compute buyer mainly pay for?
quiz.why: Compute is sold as reserved capacity, committed ahead of use.

quiz.prompt: Why is an oversized commit risky for the seller?
options: Unused capacity becomes a churn risk at renewal
quiz.why: A customer paying for idle capacity is unlikely to renew at the same size.

quiz.prompt: Which threat turns the deal into a price fight?
quiz.why: Comparing raw price per FLOP ignores the value you deliver on top.
